subject: community-medicine
title: Socialisation, Culture, Family Types, and Social Class

steps.title: Socialisation: learning to belong
steps.tx: **Socialisation** is the lifelong process by which a person acquires the language, norms, values, skills, and roles of their society, beginning in the family (primary socialisation) and continuing through school, peers, workplaces, and media (secondary socialisation). Health behaviour is socialised early: food habits, hygiene, tobacco norms, and care seeking scripts are absorbed long before any clinic visit teaches them.
steps.say: Socialisation teaches us how our society eats, cleans, smokes, and seeks care. Families write the first and deepest draft.

nodes.label: Adult roles and health habits stabilise

steps.title: Culture and health behaviour
steps.tx: **Culture in medical sociology** is the learned, shared way of life of a group: beliefs about hot and cold foods in illness, evil eye explanations of disease, fasting practices, and food taboos in pregnancy. Culture is not ignorance to be scolded but the operating system every health message must run on. Acculturation describes adopting a new culture's traits on migration, with diet and disease patterns shifting within a generation.
steps.say: Culture is the software health messages must run on. Work with food beliefs and illness explanations, not against them.

steps.title: Types of family
steps.tx: Sociology classifies the **types of family in health practice**: nuclear (couple with unmarried children), joint (multiple related couples and kin sharing roof, kitchen, and purse), extended, three generation, single parent, and broken families where a parent has died or deserted. The family is the unit of health care in Indian practice because decisions, money, and caregiving pool inside it.
steps.say: Nuclear, joint, extended, broken: family form decides who pays, decides, and nurses. Treat the family, not just the patient.

rows: Related couples, common kitchen and purse

steps.title: Joint family: health balance sheet
steps.tx: The **joint family system** pools income, childcare, and elder care, buffers crises, and enforces health norms, at the cost of crowding, shared infections, less privacy for contraception counselling, and slower decisions when elders veto modern care. Urbanisation and migration are nuclearising Indian households measurably in census and survey rounds, shifting caregiving burdens onto smaller units.
steps.say: Joint families buffer illness costs and care for elders, but crowd infections in and privacy out. Cities are nuclearising fast.

right.title: Joint family costs
points: Elder veto can delay modern care

steps.tx: Grandparents, parents and children cook in one kitchen in a **joint family**. Wages, childcare and the care of the old are pooled, and an illness is noticed because someone is always at home. The same rooms pass respiratory and skin infection from one generation to the next, and a younger woman may not discuss contraception while elders are in the room. Census rounds show more of these households splitting as work shifts to the cities.
steps.say: Three generations share income, childcare and care of the old, and they also share infections. Privacy for contraception is limited. Migration is splitting more of these households into smaller ones.

steps.title: Family cycle and vulnerable phases
steps.tx: Families move through a **family life cycle**: formation, extension with children, complete extension, contraction as children leave, and dissolution. Health risks cluster by phase: young extension strains maternal and child services, contraction brings empty nest loneliness, and dissolution leaves widowed elders destitute. Community workers who map households by phase anticipate needs (immunisation versus elder care) before crises announce them.
steps.say: Each family phase carries predictable health needs. Map the phase and you can predict the service before the crisis.

steps.title: Social class and health gradients
steps.tx: **Social class** (grouping by occupation, income, education, and prestige) predicts health with brutal regularity: lower classes suffer higher mortality, malnutrition, and exposure, and use preventive services less, the inverse care law. Indian scales operationalise class for research: Kuppuswamy (urban) and BG Prasad (income based) dominate, detailed in the next lesson. Class is a confounder in nearly every epidemiological analysis.
steps.say: Lower class means sicker and less served: the inverse care law. Measure class in every community study or be confounded by it.

steps.title: Kuppuswamy scale introduced
steps.tx: The **Kuppuswamy socioeconomic scale** scores the head of family's education (one to seven), occupation (one to ten), and monthly family income (one to twelve), summing to classes from upper (twenty six to twenty nine) to lower (below five). Built for urban families, it needs income revision with inflation (consumer price index linking), the maintenance task students most often forget.
steps.say: Kuppuswamy adds education, occupation, and income scores for urban families. Update the income bands or the scale rots.

steps.title: Social mobility and social pathology
steps.tx: Movement between classes (social mobility) through education and occupation reshapes health within a generation, while **social pathology** studies community level diseases of society: alcoholism, drug dependence, suicide, juvenile delinquency, and prostitution as social diagnoses needing social treatment. Community medicine claims these because their causes and cures sit in families, markets, and laws more than in clinics.
steps.say: Addiction and suicide are social pathology: caused socially, cured socially. Clinics alone cannot close that loop.

steps.title: Doctor as social scientist
steps.tx: The closing frame is the **doctor patient relationship in society**: Parsons cast the doctor as applied scientist and the patient in a sick role (detailed next lesson), while Indian practice adds family negotiation, plural medical systems (AYUSH, informal providers), and payment at point of care. Cultural competence (asking what the patient believes caused this illness) is a clinical skill with measurable effects on adherence.
steps.say: Ask what the patient believes caused the illness. That one question aligns your prescription with their world.
